content: MUST-CHECK: archiveOlderThan in scripts/lib/store.ts compares e.ts < cutoffTs (strict less-than). An entry created in the same second as an archive --days 0 call will NOT be archived because its ts equals (not less than) the cutoff. Tests exercising --days 0 or small day windows must seed entries with an explicit past ts (e.g. now - 3600) via direct JSONL write, not rely on wall-clock timing.

CLI numeric flags (kb.ts --days/--since/--limit) must be validated with a digits-only regex (all-digit test) BEFORE calling Number(raw). Number() alone accepts floats, hex (0x10), exponents (1e3), trailing dots (3.), and coerces empty/whitespace strings to 0 -- all of which are dangerous when the value feeds a cutoff calculation (e.g. archive --days). The single shared validator (parseNonNegInt in scripts/kb.ts) is the only call site for all three numeric flags.

MUST-CHECK: In scripts/kb.ts parseFlags, a flag with no consumable value stores boolean true, not a string. Guards like `typeof flags.x === "string"` silently skip validation and fall through to defaults for that flag, which is dangerous for destructive commands (e.g. archive --days with a swallowed/empty value defaulted to 90 instead of erroring). Always add an explicit `if (flags.x === true) { error; return 1; }` guard before the string-type check for any flag whose absence has a meaningfully different behavior than a present-but-empty value.

MUST-CHECK: A test that only asserts the post-condition of a destructive/cleanup operation (e.g. "store is empty after archive") is vacuously true if the seed data never landed (wrong file path, bad fixture). Always assert the pre-state (seed count before the call) and/or a positive post-state (e.g. archive now contains N entries), not just the negative absence.

MUST-CHECK: the drawbar kb store's active file is knowledge.jsonl (archive: knowledge.archive.jsonl), per storePaths() in scripts/lib/store.ts. When hand-building a shell harness to verify archive/compact behavior, seeding a file named active.jsonl (or any other guess) leaves the real store EMPTY, so every destructive command reports success against nothing and the store-preserved assertion passes vacuously. Verified this the hard way while reviewing PCO-339: an 8-vector wipe test appeared to pass with the store intact, but the store was never populated. Always seed via the real filename, or via ensureDir(dir).active, and assert a non-zero pre-state count before the destructive call.

MUST-CHECK: scripts/kb.ts compact uses flags["dry-run"] === true, so `kb compact --dry-run 1` binds the string "1", the === true test is false, and a REAL compaction runs while the operator believes they are previewing. This is the mirror image of the PCO-339 --days bug: there a boolean-where-string-expected failed open, here a string-where-boolean-expected fails open. Data-preserving (losers go to the archive, recoverable via recall --all) and pre-existing, so it was left out of PCO-339 scope. Belongs to PCO-340/S2, whose LD5 mandates flag type enforcement in BOTH directions. The same latent shape exists for recall --all and --json, but those fail in the narrowing direction and are not an exposure.

MUST-CHECK: when writing tests that assert bm25(kb) ranking order for OR-joined multi-token FTS5 queries, do not assume the entry matching more distinct query tokens always ranks first, or that ts breaks ties in the direction you expect. bm25 favors rows matching rarer terms (lower doc frequency) over rows matching more common terms, even if another row matches more total tokens. Verify actual ranking with a throwaway script against the real fixture before hardcoding expected order in a test.

MUST-CHECK: FTS5 bm25() ranking sorts by term rarity (IDF), not by how many query tokens a row matches. A row matching one rare token can outrank a row matching two common tokens (near-zero IDF each). Do not name/comment tests as "matches more tokens ranks higher" -- isolate rarity vs token-count as independent variables when writing ranking fixtures, or the test will pass for the wrong reason.

fts5 bm25 clamps a non-positive IDF to 1e-6 rather than 0. Even when every matched term is common (df == N), bm25 stays a strictly ordered function of term frequency and document length at a tiny magnitude — it never actually ties, so ts DESC is never reached as a general fallback for common-term queries. ts DESC only breaks bit-identical bm25 values, which requires structurally symmetric rows (same doc length, same df/tf per matched term). Do not describe common-term bm25 behavior as falling back to recency.

MUST-CHECK: a bm25 test claiming to prove term-rarity dominance (rare token beats a doc matching two common tokens) must hold document length EQUAL between the two compared rows, or document-length normalization (shorter docs score better) can produce the same ranking for the wrong reason, and a one-word edit to a fixture string can silently flip the result. Verify by sweeping the non-length-controlled document's word count across a wide range (we used 1-20 words) and confirming the ranking never flips before trusting the test.

MUST-CHECK: when hand-writing a probe to verify a test's behavior outside the test runner, replicate the ENTIRE fixture, including whatever beforeEach seeds. A partial fixture can silently invert the conclusion. Hit twice in one session: (1) seeded a store file named active.jsonl when the real one is knowledge.jsonl, so a destructive-command check passed against an empty store (see [[kb-store-active-file-is-knowledge-jsonl]]); (2) probed a bm25 ranking claim with only the 4 entries the test appends, omitting the 3 the describe block's beforeEach seeds -- N=4 instead of N=7 changed every document frequency and produced the OPPOSITE result, wrongly clearing a reviewer finding that was in fact correct. Corollary for FTS/bm25 specifically: document frequency is a property of the whole table, so ANY entry present changes ranking. Re-probe against real conditions before accepting or rejecting a ranking claim.

MUST-CHECK: before moving a drawbar story to In Progress and dispatching an implementer, verify the paths in the story's ## Files section are actually WRITABLE from this session, not merely readable. A directory can be listed as an additional working directory, be owned by the user, show drwxr-xr-x with no ACLs, and still return EPERM (Operation not permitted) on every write — the harness sandbox profile is applied at process spawn and dangerouslyDisableSandbox does NOT lift it. Hit on PCO-346, whose entire diff lands in /Users/mjn/workplace/mikes_env: git checkout -b failed with "cannot lock ref ... unable to create directory", and a plain touch of any file under the repo failed the same way, while the primary working dir was writable. Cheap probe: touch <dir>/.probe && rm <dir>/.probe. Doing this in the prerequisite gate (step 3) costs one command and saves burning a Sonnet implementer against a read-only tree — the failure mode looks like a git error, not a permissions error, so it is easy to misdiagnose as a bad branch name.
